nameStory: Common spikerush gets its name from its distinctive flower spike that sits like a tiny club at the tip of each slender stem. The "spike" refers to the compact, egg-shaped flower head, while "rush" comes from its resemblance to true rushes, though it's actually a sedge. The scientific name "palustris" means "of the marsh," pointing to its love of wet places.
description: Common spikerush is a mat-forming wetland plant that creates dense colonies of slender, green stems rising from creeping underground rhizomes. Each pencil-thin stem is topped with a single, compact flower spike that looks like a tiny brown egg or club. The stems are typically 6-20 inches tall and have no visible leaves - just smooth, round stems that do all the photosynthesis. It's part of the sedge family, not a true rush, and spreads to form extensive carpets in marshy areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single egg-shaped spike at tip of each stem, about the size of a small grape, brown to rusty-colored when mature with tiny individual flowers packed tightly together

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense mats or colonies of upright stems from creeping underground rhizomes, creating carpet-like patches in wet areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, round, leafless stems that feel firm and slightly spongy when squeezed, bright green and doing the work of leaves

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: No visible leaves above ground - just brownish sheaths wrapped around the base of stems at soil level

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny lens-shaped seeds with small bristles, produced within the flower spike after blooming

habitat: Look for common spikerush in shallow water, marshes, wet meadows, pond edges, and muddy shores throughout New England. It thrives in areas that are seasonally flooded or consistently moist, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants. You'll find it from sea level to mountain ponds, in both fresh and slightly brackish water.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from underground rhizomes as water warms, growing rapidly in the longer daylight hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with flower spikes developing and maturing from green to brown, creating the most distinctive identification features.
seasonality.fall: Stems begin to yellow and die back, with seeds dispersing from the brown spikes before plants go dormant.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only underground rhizomes alive beneath the ice and snow.

funFact: Common spikerush can actually help clean polluted water - its dense root systems filter out excess nutrients and toxins, making it a natural water treatment plant that wetland restoration projects often use to improve water quality.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spikerush species in the same genus, but common spikerush typically forms the densest colonies and has the most robust stems. True rushes have visible leaves and different flower arrangements, while grasses have completely different flower structures with no single terminal spike.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "rush," this plant is actually a sedge, which explains the old botanical saying "sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses have joints when the stems are found." The name confusion comes from early botanists grouping similar-looking wetland plants together before understanding their true relationships.
compareHints: Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes. Needle spikerush is much more delicate with hair-thin stems, while blunt spikerush has more egg-shaped spikes and doesn't form such extensive mats. Most other spikerush species in our region are smaller, more scattered, or have distinctly different spike shapes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
